title: Training-Free Vector Quantization via Gaussian VAEs
one_liner: Train a smooth Gaussian model to learn image structure, then snap its soft outputs to discrete tokens without retraining.
lead: Images are stored as discrete tokens (like words in a book). To compress an image into tokens, you need a machine that learns to split it into chunks and label each one with a number. The problem: teaching machines to use discrete tokens is slow and temperamental. This paper skips the hard training step entirely. Instead it trains a Gaussian autoencoder (a smooth machine that outputs real numbers), then snaps those real numbers to discrete tokens in one step. No retraining needed.

problem.h2: Why discrete tokens are so hard to train
paras: Imagine you want to compress a photo into a sequence of codewords—like assigning each patch to the closest entry in a giant lookup table. The naive approach trains the machine end-to-end: the encoder learns to map image patches to codebook vectors, the decoder reconstructs from those vectors. But the discrete snapping (picking the closest codeword) has no gradient—there is no smooth slope to follow during training. So you have to bolt on extra tricks: soft relaxations, commitment losses, and penalties that keep each output from dropping too low or spiking too high. Each trick adds complexity, bugs, and hyperparameter tuning.

Every existing VQ-VAE (a machine that compresses images by turning them into discrete codeword labels) fights this rounding-to-discrete problem. The machine ends up half-trained because the discrete step is a hard wall.

callout.html: Train a smooth Gaussian autoencoder with a per-dimension KL budget, then snap its outputs to discrete tokens using pre-drawn random codebook in one shot, with no retraining.

panels.title: 1. The problem
panels.caption: Old way: train encoder/decoder to predict discrete tokens. Gradient gets stuck at the hard snapping wall.

panels.title: 2. Gaussian smooth version
panels.caption: New idea: replace discrete machine with smooth Gaussian outputs. Each dimension now has its own KL budget.

panels.title: 3. Constrain each dimension
panels.viz_args: Each dimension: target KL = log(codebook_size). Penalty if it overshoots or undershoots.
panels.caption: The per-dimension KL constraint (TDC) steers encoder spreads to match discrete bit budget.

panels.title: 4. Draw random codebook once
panels.caption: Snap each smooth output to nearest random Gaussian noise vector. One shot, no retraining.

panels.title: 5. Done: discrete tokens ready
panels.caption: Reconstruction quality matches full VQ-VAE training but in a fraction of the time.

steps.text: Gaussian autoencoder with per-dimension KL control learns image structure as real numbers.
Sample random Gaussian noise vectors (one per discrete label) as the lookup table.
For each encoded image, snap each dimension to its nearest codebook vector.
Decoder reconstructs the image from discrete token indices.
Done. The snapping is one-way; nothing adjusts after conversion.

paras: The paper replaces the hard discrete training loop (with its temperamental loss tricks) with a two-stage recipe: train a smooth Gaussian autoencoder, then convert it to discrete tokens in one shot.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: per-dimension KL divergence
hidden.name: KL divergence per hidden dimension
paras: KL divergence (Kullback-Leibler divergence) is a measure of how different two probability distributions are—how many extra bits you need to encode samples from one distribution if your code was built for the other. In this paper, the hidden quantity is the KL divergence per hidden dimension: for each output value the encoder produces, how far is its spread from the standard Gaussian used in a plain VAE (a standard-shaped bell curve). If the KL is too high, that dimension is using more than its share of bits; too low, it is wasting bits.

The paper estimates KL for each dimension during Gaussian VAE training and penalizes dimensions that overshoot or undershoot a target budget (the target divergence constraint, or TDC). This forces the encoder to use each dimension's capacity consistently, so when you snap to discrete tokens, every dimension carries about the same amount of information.

heat.caption: Darker color means higher KL divergence (using more bits). Highlighted dimensions exceed or undershoot the target; TDC penalty nudges them back.

reads.html: Each hidden dimension needs to allocate its probability budget equally. Dimensions that hoard bits get penalized; dimensions that waste bits also get penalized. This balance is what makes the one-shot rounding work.

For each hidden dimension i, compute its KL divergence using the encoder distribution and compare to a target bits budget log(K). Penalize if KL exceeds log(K) plus a tolerance alpha, or falls short by alpha. This per-dimension rate control is the target divergence constraint.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the causal chain
paras: The core insight is that discrete rounding (snapping to the nearest value) works cleanly only if the input data is already well-distributed. In this paper, the Gaussian autoencoder is trained to output values spread over a specific range with a specific density. The TDC constraint ensures that each hidden dimension has learned to pack its information into a standard Gaussian shape, calibrated to a specific bit budget. When you generate random Gaussian noise as the codebook, those random points already sit in the right places—the encoder outputs naturally cluster near them.

Because the Gaussian autoencoder has already learned the task of compression (finding structure in the image), and its outputs are already shaped to match discrete bits, snapping to the nearest codebook vector is almost a no-operation. The encoder has already done the hard work of learning which parts of the image matter and how to split it into chunks. Discretization becomes a formality, not a training bottleneck.

stages.s: Encoder outputs soft Gaussian for each dimension
TDC training ensures outputs match bit budget
Snap each soft value to nearest discrete codeword

math.words: For each latent dimension i, the training loss penalizes the KL divergence if it strays from the target budget. Loss = reconstruction error plus a weighted penalty on each dimension's KL, where the weight is larger if KL exceeds the target plus a margin (alpha) or falls short.
math.equation: L_TDC = reconstruction_loss + sum_i [ (lambda_over if KL_i > log(K) + alpha else lambda_under) * (KL_i - log(K))^2 ]
symbols: divergence for latent dimension i (how many extra bits that dimension uses)
target bits per dimension, where K is codebook size
tolerance band (how much overshoot/undershoot is allowed before penalty kicks in)
penalty weight if dimension uses too many bits
penalty weight if dimension wastes bits

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Codebook size K = 4 (need log(4) = 2 bits per dimension). Tolerance alpha = 0.2.
Dimension 1: actual KL = 2.5. Overshoots target by 0.5 (> alpha). Penalty = lambda_over * (2.5 - 2)^2 = 2.0 * 0.25 = 0.5.
Dimension 2: actual KL = 1.9. Undershoots target by 0.1 (< alpha). No penalty.
Dimension 3: actual KL = 1.95. Undershoots by 0.05 (< alpha). No penalty.
During training, dimension 1 gets gradient signal to reduce its KL; dimensions 2 and 3 stay as is. By end of training, all three cluster around KL = 2, so discretization is consistent.

math.note: The TDC loss steers each dimension to use exactly its share of bits, so when you snap to random codebook points, information density is uniform and quantization loses almost nothing.

charts.title: Old VQ-VAE training
charts.note: Discrete training is slow and flaky. Many weights are never updated.

charts.title: Gaussian Quant (this paper)
charts.note: Smooth training converges fast. One-shot rounding gets codebook utilization and quality both higher.

items.b: Gaussian VAE not trained with TDC.
items.html: If you train a plain Gaussian VAE without the per-dimension KL budget, its dimensions will be unbalanced—some will hoard bits, others waste them. When you snap to random codebook vectors, those random points won't land well, and reconstruction degrades. Always use TDC.

If the codebook has fewer codewords than the theory requires (log of codebook size must exceed the VAE's bits-back rate), rounding error grows. The paper proves this but you have to pick the codebook size large enough.
Codebook is random Gaussian noise. A bad random seed can produce codebook points that are outliers or clustered unevenly. Averaging over multiple codebooks reduces this risk.
Train Gaussian VAE with TDC, use large enough codebook, generate codebook carefully. Then one-shot rounding reconstructs accurately without any retraining loop.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small autoencoder on CIFAR-10 (32x32 color images). Train a Gaussian VAE with the target divergence constraint for 50 epochs on half the dataset. Then, without any further training, generate a random Gaussian codebook and round the learned encoder outputs to the nearest discrete tokens. Measure reconstruction error on a held-out test set.
demo.metric_eq: reconstruction_error = mean_absolute_error(original_image, decoded_quantized_image); codebook_usage = fraction_of_codewords_actually_used_in_test_set; time_saved = (training_time_for_old_VQ_VAE) minus (training_time_for_Gaussian_VAE_plus_quantization)
demo.closing: The demo must show that per-dimension KL control makes quantization accurate without retraining—and that you achieve codebook usage above 90 percent (nearly all codewords are used) in a single pass.
